title: The potter (Jeremiah 18)
hook: a vessel spoiled in the potter's hand is made again

segments.voice: Yesterday, a young man named Jeremiah, shown the shaqed, said I'm only a child, and God said before I formed thee in the belly, I knew thee. Your line was known before the womb. Did you remember it once? Day four hundred twenty-two.

Anyone who has tried a pottery class knows the moment. The clay is spinning, it's rising, it actually looks like a bowl, and then one wobble and the whole wall folds over like a tired flower. The instructor doesn't hand you new clay. She says: squash it, wet it, center it again. Jeremiah watched that moment about twenty-six centuries ago. God sent him on an errand with no explanation: go down to the potter's house, and you'll hear my words there. So he went, and stood in a workshop, and watched a craftsman ruin a pot.
screen: `ONE WOBBLE, AND THE BOWL FOLDS.` → `GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.` → `A PROPHET WATCHES A POT FAIL.`

segments.voice: The scene is Jeremiah chapter eighteen, Jeremias in the Douay-Rheims. The potter is working at his wheel, and the vessel he's shaping goes wrong in his hands. Spoiled. And he doesn't throw the clay out. He gathers it up and makes another vessel from the same lump, as it seemed good to him to make it. Then the word comes, and it's a question first: can't I do with you what this potter does? And then the Douay: "Behold as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel." Two things are true at once in that workshop. The clay is soft, so it can go wrong. And because it's still soft, it can be made again. There's a word hiding here from yesterday. The Hebrew for potter, yotser, means one who forms. It comes from the same verb as before I formed thee. The God who formed Jeremiah in the womb is the potter still at the wheel. Jeremiah's message wasn't only comfort, though. The next verses are a warning to a whole nation: if a people turns from its evil, God will relent; if it turns from good, the good is taken back. And in the very next chapter Jeremiah buys a finished, fired jar and smashes it in front of the elders. A fired pot can't be reworked. Many Catholics think of this chapter when they bring what has gone wrong to God, in the sacrament of penance, in an evening examen, in a quiet church. The pot that slumped isn't the end of the clay.
screen: `THE VESSEL SPOILED ON THE WHEEL.` · `HE MAKES ANOTHER FROM THE SAME CLAY.` · `YOTSER: THE ONE WHO FORMS.` · `A FIRED JAR CAN'T BE REWORKED.` · then, large: `AS CLAY IS IN THE HAND OF THE POTTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer up something spoiled. Settle, and breathe. Cup your hands in your lap, as if you were holding a lump of wet clay. Now let something that went wrong come to mind. A conversation that collapsed. A habit that slumped. A plan that folded over on the wheel. Don't fix it. Just put it in your hands and look at it. It's still soft. If you pray, you can hold your hands out and give it back to God as it is. If you don't, just notice that it isn't fired yet. The bell holds the time.
The potter. In Jeremiah, the craftsman who doesn't throw away spoiled clay but makes it into another vessel. Today's word.
Your line: made again. Today, go back to one thing that went wrong and give it one more turn of the wheel. Day four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics bring what has gone wrong in their lives to God in the sacrament of penance and in daily prayer, and Jeremiah's visit to the potter's house is among the readings at weekday Mass.

original.note: Hebrew: potter, literally one who forms, from the same verb as before I formed thee (Jeremiah 1:5).

trapdoor: what you thought: God as a craftsman, a nice picture.
what it means: a spoiled pot isn't thrown away but made again from the same clay, while it's still soft; and a warning that a fired jar can be broken.
what a scholar hears: yotser, the one who forms, from yatsar, the verb of Genesis 2:7 and Jeremiah 1:5. the potter of chapter 18 is the former of chapter 1.

sources.quoted: Behold as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel.
